docs.title: CVE-2026-112082 — SGLang: Unauthenticated DoS via the Expert-Distribution Recording Endpoint
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product sgl-project/sglang up to 0.5.19 — Scheduler.expert_distribution_handle (python/sglang/srt/eplb/expert_distribution.py) Type Improper input handling leading to denial of service (no CWE assigned yet) Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction → one crafted request crashes the inference server; exploit is public; fix PR still pending

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • SGLang <= 0.5.19. Upstream fix: PR #42098 (awaiting acceptance — no released patch yet).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The expert-distribution recording endpoint (expert_distribution_handle) processes attacker-influenced fields without sufficient validation. A single remote, unauthenticated request carrying a manipulated payload drives the scheduler into a crash — taking down the inference server and every model it serves. The exploit is publicly available while the official fix is still an unmerged pull request.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def expert_distribution_handle(request):
    record = parse(request.payload)   # no validation
    scheduler.apply(record.weights)   # crash on malformed data

# Simplified fixed pattern
def expert_distribution_handle(request):
    record = parse(request.payload)
    if not valid_distribution(record):
        return 400
    scheduler.apply(record.weights)

docs.text:
1. The attacker reaches the SGLang server's recording endpoint over the network — no login needed.
  2. They send one request with a manipulated expert-distribution payload.
  3. The scheduler crashes → denial of service for all inference traffic on that server.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: an unvalidated handler versus a validating one, against a synthetic offline scheduler. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.text:
• Firewall the debug/admin ports now — do not expose SGLang's recording endpoints to untrusted networks.
  • Track PR #42098 and upgrade as soon as a fixed release ships.
  • Front the inference tier with authentication / a reverse proxy plus request-size limits.
  • Monitor for crashes correlated with requests to the recording endpoint.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112146 — D-Link EAGLE PRO AI routers: hard-coded MQTT broker credentials
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.1 7.4 Product D-Link E15, M32, R15, R32 (EAGLE PRO AI mesh routers) Type Hard-coded credentials — CWE-259 / CWE-798 Attack vector Remote (network), low attack complexity, low privileges required

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: D-Link EAGLE PRO AI mesh line models E15, M32, R15 and R32 with firmware whose /etc/emDaemon/passwd (MQTT Broker component) carries the factory-baked credential. Check D-Link's support page for your hardware revision and install the latest firmware as updates ship.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The MQTT broker inside the router authenticates with a credential stored in /etc/emDaemon/passwd. That credential is hard-coded into the firmware image, so every unit of every affected model shares the exact same password. Anyone who recovers the credential from one firmware dump can authenticate to the MQTT broker of any deployed router. The NVD record notes the exploit is now public.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual attack chain (educational only — no working exploit):

  1. Firmware extraction. The attacker downloads the router firmware from D-Link's support site and unpacks the image offline.
  2. Credential recovery. Inside the filesystem image, the file /etc/emDaemon/passwd is found carrying the same credential that ships on every unit.
  3. Reuse across the fleet. Because the secret never varies per device, that one credential authenticates to the MQTT broker of any E15, M32, R15 or R32 reachable on the network.
  4. Broker access. With broker access the attacker can observe mesh node chatter (status, configuration) and inject messages into the control plane — the vulnerable pattern below versus the fixed pattern:
# VULNERABLE pattern: one secret baked into every firmware image
CREDENTIAL = load_from("/etc/emDaemon/passwd")   # identical on every unit

# FIXED pattern: a unique secret generated per device at first boot
CREDENTIAL = load_from("/etc/emDaemon/passwd")    # generated once, per device

This writeup deliberately does not reproduce the public exploit. Do not test against devices you do not own; only ever test in controlled environments.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update firmware: check D-Link's official support page for your exact model and hardware revision; install security updates the moment one ships.
  • Isolate the IoT network: place routers and IoT devices on a separate VLAN/SSID from personal devices.
  • Disable remote management: keep the admin interface and the MQTT broker off the WAN; restrict management to trusted local systems.
  • Watch for oddities: failed authentication attempts, unexpected config changes, or routers dropping off the mesh.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112264 — BentoML Dockerfile Instruction Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (CVSS 4.0 8.5 / CVSS 3.1 7.8) Product BentoML ≤ 1.4.39 (ML model serving framework) Type OS command / Dockerfile instruction injection (CWE-78) Attack vector Local — a crafted bentofile.yaml or an imported bento archive consumed by bentoml containerize

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: BentoML through 1.4.39.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: BentoML generates a Dockerfile when you run bentoml containerize. The legacy Jinja template src/bentoml/_internal/container/frontend/dockerfile/templates/base.j2 renders the docker.env mapping (from src/bentoml/_internal/bento/build_config.py) directly into the Dockerfile without validating the keys. In Dockerfile syntax, a newline ends one instruction and begins another — so a mapping key containing an embedded newline breaks out of the intended ENV line and lets an attacker add arbitrary build instructions (e.g. a RUN line) to the generated Dockerfile. Those injected instructions then execute during docker build, where they can read build secrets and poison the resulting image.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
Attack chain:

  1. Attacker publishes a model or shares a bento archive whose bentofile.yaml contains a docker.env mapping with a key that hides a newline, for example MODEL_NAME\nRUN <cmd>.
  2. Victim imports the bento and runs bentoml containerize.
  3. The legacy base.j2 template renders the key verbatim, so the generated Dockerfile now contains an attacker-controlled RUN instruction.
  4. docker build executes it with full build context — build secrets, tokens, and the ability to bake a backdoored model into the shipped image.

Vulnerable vs. fixed pattern:

# VULNERABLE — key copied verbatim into the Dockerfile template
ENV {{ key }}={{ value }}        # key == "MODEL_NAME\nRUN <cmd>" injects a new instruction

# FIXED — keys are validated before rendering
def env_line(key, value):
    if "\n" in key or "\r" in key or not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z0-9_]+", key):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid env key: {key!r}")
    return f"ENV {key}={value}"

Educational only: this describes the mechanism and the fix. It is not a working exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade BentoML past 1.4.39 to the fixed release.
  • Only run bentoml containerize on bentos you built yourself or obtained from sources you trust.
  • Manually inspect any third-party bentofile.yaml (especially docker.env keys) before building.
  • Rebuild any image that was produced from an untrusted bento; treat it as potentially tainted.
  • In CI/CD, validate all bento archives at ingest time and restrict build-secret scope.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112266 — SGLang: Cross-Request Abort via rid Prefix Matching
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.2 Product SGLang ≤ 0.5.22 (LLM serving engine) Type Denial of Service — partial string comparison (CWE-187) Vector Unauthenticated remote API clients abort other users' in-flight /generate requests

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: SGLang through 0.5.22. Fixed in versions past 0.5.22 (apply the upstream patch).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Every generation request carries a client-controlled rid (request ID). When a streaming client disconnects, the scheduler's abort path matches in-flight requests by prefix (rid.startswith(abort_rid)) instead of comparing the exact ID. A request ID is not the same as an identity check — the server treats one character of user input as a valid cancellation selector, so a disconnect for rid "a" aborts every request whose rid begins with "a": other users' chatbots, agents, and copilots all die mid-stream.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker opens streaming /generate requests with single hex-character rids ("a", "3").
  2. Attacker disconnects immediately.
  3. The abort handler prefix-matches the rid and kills all requests starting with that character.
  4. Repeat across the hex alphabet → whole server's in-flight queue is wiped.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable prefix-match abort versus the exact-match fix, against a synthetic offline mock scheduler. No exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade SGLang past 0.5.22. Enforce exact-match request IDs in the abort path. Prefer server-generated unique rids so clients cannot choose collisions. Rate-limit/abort-throttle per client.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112269 — SGLang Mooncake: Memory Exhaustion via Unauthenticated Decode Registrations
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 Product SGLang ≤ 0.5.22 with Mooncake disaggregation backend Type Denial of Service — uncontrolled resource allocation (CWE-770) Vector Network-adjacent attackers send unauthenticated decode registrations to the Prefill ZMQ PULL socket

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: SGLang through 0.5.22 (Mooncake disaggregation backend). Fixed in versions past 0.5.22 (apply the upstream patch).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The Prefill rank's ZMQ PULL socket accepts decode registration messages with no authentication. Each registration carries a mooncake_session_id plus large nested-buffer frames, and the handler stores them in memory without limits. A network-adjacent attacker simply sends many registrations with unique session IDs, and Prefill memory grows unboundedly until the scheduler is OOM-killed. Internal control-plane traffic was trusted on arrival — no auth, no caps, no rate limits.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker learns the Prefill rank address.
  2. Attacker sends decode registration messages with fresh mooncake_session_id values and large nested buffers.
  3. No authentication is required; every message allocates memory.
  4. Prefill memory is exhausted → scheduler OOM-killed → service down.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable unbounded registration handler versus an authenticated, memory-capped one, against a synthetic offline mock. No exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade SGLang past 0.5.22. Authenticate internal control-plane messages (or bind ZMQ sockets to localhost). Cap memory per session and total registrations. Rate-limit and expire stale sessions.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112270 — SGLang Mooncake: OOM via Unbounded chunk_idx in handle_staging_rsp()
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 Product SGLang ≤ 0.5.22 with Mooncake disaggregation backend Type Denial of Service — uncontrolled memory allocation (CWE-770) Vector Network-adjacent attackers send STAGING_RSP messages with huge chunk_idx under fresh room IDs

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: SGLang through 0.5.22 (Mooncake disaggregation backend). Fixed in versions past 0.5.22 (apply the upstream patch).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: handle_staging_rsp() allocates memory based on the attacker-controlled chunk_idx field of incoming STAGING_RSP messages, with no bounds checking. The rank address is discoverable from the public /route endpoint, so a network-adjacent attacker sends staging responses carrying enormous chunk_idx values under fresh room IDs. Each message triggers a massive allocation, Prefill memory is exhausted, and the scheduler is OOM-killed. The pattern is the same disease as its sibling CVE-2026-112269: internal messages are trusted on arrival — no auth, no range validation.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker reads the rank address from the /route endpoint.
  2. Attacker crafts STAGING_RSP messages with huge chunk_idx under fresh room IDs.
  3. handle_staging_rsp() allocates memory proportional to chunk_idx — unchecked.

docs.title: CVE-2026-16460 — bootc + ostree: Two Holes in the OS Image Trust Chain (Signature Bypass)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.4 (CVE-2026-16460), CVSS 8.1 (CVE-2026-16487) Product bootc + ostree — image-based Linux (RHEL image mode, Fedora Atomic) Type Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity (CWE-345) Vector Local (16460: staged deployments) / Network (16487: mutable-tag upgrades) → unsigned OS content becomes the host on reboot

This writeup covers two CVEs published together against the same product:

CVE Issue CVE-2026-16460 bootc and ostree finalize already-staged deployments without revalidating the container image against the current containers signature policy. Unsigned OS content staged under a prior permissive policy stays bootable after the policy is hardened to reject unsigned images. CVSS 7.4, AV:L/AC:H. CVE-2026-16487 bootc operating with the default containers signature policy: automatic or manual upgrades of a mutable image tag may apply unsigned content for registries that fall through to insecureAcceptAnything. An attacker who can update that tag gets arbitrary OS content executed as the host root filesystem on reboot. CVSS 8.1, AV:N/AC:H.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• CVE-2026-16460: bootc/ostree builds predating the upstream fix — staged deployments are finalized without policy revalidation. Track the fix via the Red Hat CVE page.
  • CVE-2026-16487: bootc builds honoring the default containers signature policy with insecureAcceptAnything fallthrough. Track the fix via the Red Hat CVE page.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A signature-policy decision is made once, at pull time, and then trusted forever. Two code paths skip the check at the moments that matter:

  1. Finalize path (CVE-2026-16460): the policy is consulted when content is staged, never when the staged deployment is finalized or booted. Hardening the policy afterwards changes the rules for new pulls, but the staged deployment keeps its old, unvalidated trust — and it is still the one queued to boot.
  2. Upgrade path (CVE-2026-16487): registries with no explicit rule in the policy fall through to insecureAcceptAnything, so for those registries the signature check silently never runs — on automatic and manual upgrades of mutable tags.
# Simplified vulnerable pattern (containers policy + bootc finalize)
policy:
  default: signedBy(trusted-key)   # checked ONLY at pull/stage time
  # no rule for attacker.registry  ->  insecureAcceptAnything fallthrough

finalize(staged_deployment):
    boot(staged.image)             # <-- no policy re-check here

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
Path A (CVE-2026-16460):

  1. With the containers signature policy still permissive, unsigned OS content is staged on the machine (attacker needs local access).
  2. The admin hardens the policy to reject unsigned images. The staged deployment is untouched and stays queued to boot.
  3. On reboot, bootc finalizes the staged deployment — no revalidation — and the machine boots attacker-controlled content as the host OS. Full compromise of confidentiality, integrity and availability.

Path B (CVE-2026-16487):

  1. The machine tracks a mutable tag (e.g. registry/app:latest) on a registry with no explicit policy rule, falling through to insecureAcceptAnything.
  2. An attacker who can update that tag (registry compromise, weak credentials) points it at unsigned, malicious OS content.
  3. The next automatic or manual upgrade pulls it with no signature check; on reboot it becomes the host root filesystem.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a finalize step that skips revalidation versus one that re-checks the current policy, and a mutable tag that falls through to "accept anything" versus a pinned digest with an explicit signedBy rule. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update bootc and ostree to the patched releases (see the Red Hat CVE pages above for errata).
  • Pin images to immutable digests, not mutable tags, wherever the fleet allows it.
  • Close the policy hole: remove any insecureAcceptAnything fallthrough from your containers signature policy; give every registry an explicit signedBy rule.
  • Audit every staged deployment on the fleet after any policy change — clear unvalidated staged content before it boots.
  • Rotate any credentials/tokens that could have been exposed on a compromised host and audit boot logs for unexpected staged content.

docs.title: CVE-2026-16487 — bootc: Unsigned Mutable-Tag Upgrades via insecureAcceptAnything Fallthrough
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.1 Product bootc (image-based Linux) running under the default containers signature policy Type Insufficient verification of data authenticity (CWE-345): unsigned content accepted through the insecureAcceptAnything registry fallthrough Vector Network, high complexity, no privileges → whoever can update a mutable image tag lands arbitrary OS content that becomes the host root filesystem on reboot

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • bootc builds predating the upstream fix (see the Red Hat advisory for the fixed package versions).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Under the default containers signature policy, any registry without an explicit policy entry falls through to insecureAcceptAnything. When bootc performs an automatic or manual upgrade of a mutable image tag (e.g. :latest), it may pull and apply unsigned content from such registries. Anyone able to update that tag — a compromised registry account, a tag-mutation attack — gets arbitrary OS content staged as the next boot target, running as the host root filesystem after reboot.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def policy_for(registry, policy):
    return policy.get(registry, "insecureAcceptAnything")  # unsigned accepted

# Simplified fixed pattern
def policy_for(registry, policy):
    return policy.get(registry, "reject")  # default-deny; pin digests

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The target host runs bootc with the default policy; its registry has no explicit entry → insecureAcceptAnything.
  2. The attacker updates the mutable tag (:latest) the host tracks.
  3. The next bootc upgrade (automatic or manual) pulls the unsigned image and stages it.
  4. On reboot the attacker's image becomes the host OS — full root compromise.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a policy lookup with the insecure fallthrough versus default-deny plus digest pinning. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update bootc to the fixed build (Red Hat CVE-2026-16487 / bug 2503686).
  • Remove insecureAcceptAnything from policy.json; give every registry an explicit entry (signed or reject).
  • Pin image digests (image@sha256:...) instead of tracking mutable tags.
  • Restrict who can push to the tags your fleet tracks, and monitor tag mutations.

docs.title: CVE-2026-57155 — OPNsense GeoIP Importer Path Traversal
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical 9.9 (CVSS 3.1) Product OPNsense Firewall — GeoIP importer Type Path traversal (CWE-22) → remote code execution as root Attack vector Network · low privileges (firewall alias edit rights)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: OPNsense versions prior to 26.1.11. Fixed in 26.1.11.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The GeoIP country importer takes the country_code value straight from the downloaded archive and concatenates it into a filesystem path — with no validation at all:

out = GEODIR + country + '-IPv4'
open(out, 'w')   # country is attacker-controlled

A value like ../../cron.d/evil walks out of the GeoIP directory. The importer runs as root, so the attacker's file lands anywhere on the system with root ownership.

The chain completes with a crafted log configuration plus an oversized log file, which tricks the hourly root cron job into executing the attacker's commands.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
poc.py is an educational illustration of the flawed pattern versus the fix. It runs safely — string-level only, no real filesystem writes.

python3 poc.py

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker hosts a malicious GeoIP archive on their own server.
  2. With firewall alias edit rights, they point the GeoIP source at it.
  3. The archive carries country_code = ../../cron.d/evil.
  4. The root importer writes the file outside the GeoIP folder.
  5. A crafted log config + oversized log makes the hourly root cron run it.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to OPNsense 26.1.11 — the complete fix (input is validated before any path is built).
  • Until then: restrict who can edit firewall aliases, use only trusted GeoIP sources, and keep the management interface off the internet.

docs.title: CVE-2026-76740 — HPE RMC: OS Command Injection on the Management Controller
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.2 Product HPE Compute Scale-up Server 3200/3250, HPE Superdome Flex, Superdome Flex 280 (RMC — remote management controller) Type OS Command Injection (CWE-78): management-console input interpolated unsanitized into shell commands Vector Network, low complexity, high privileges → an authenticated privileged user executes arbitrary commands on the RMC

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Firmware versions listed in HPE security bulletin hpesbhf05153 (update to the fixed firmware).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The RMC's management console takes operator input and interpolates it directly into shell commands with no neutralization. A single shell metacharacter (;, |, $(), backticks) breaks out of the intended command and executes arbitrary commands with the controller's privileges — the same controller that powers, resets, and firmware-flashes the entire rack.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def run_diagnostic(target):
    os.system(f"ping -c1 {target}")   # target = "x; id" -> breakout

# Simplified fixed pattern
def run_diagnostic(target):
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9.-]+", target):
        raise ValueError("rejected input")
    subprocess.run(["ping", "-c1", target], shell=False)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker holds a privileged RMC account (PR:H — e.g. a compromised admin credential).
  2. In a management-console field they submit a value containing a shell metacharacter.
  3. The RMC builds a shell command from the raw input and executes it.
  4. Arbitrary commands run on the controller: read or rewrite firmware, power-cycle hosts, pivot into the management network.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: string-interpolated shell invocation versus allowlist validation with shell=False. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Apply the HPE firmware update from bulletin hpesbhf05153.
  • Isolate the management network: RMC/BMC interfaces on a dedicated VLAN, never internet-exposed.
  • Harden privileged accounts: strong unique credentials, MFA where supported, least privilege, rotate after any suspected compromise.
  • Monitor RMC audit logs for unusual command patterns.

docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.2 Product Apache Camel HTTP / Netty HTTP / Undertow / Vert.x HTTP producers Type Template Injection + Information Exposure (CWE-200) Vector Inbound message headers override the endpoint URI and are template-resolved

docs.title: Mitigation

docs.title: CVE-2026-8168 — Uncontrolled recursion in Qt SVG parser/renderer (DoS)
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH (CVSS 4.0: 7.1) Product Qt SVG module (QtSvg) Type CWE-674 — Uncontrolled Recursion (stack exhaustion / stack overflow) Attack vector Network (attacker supplies a crafted SVG file; victim opens/renders it — UI:P)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Qt 4.1.0 through Qt 6.8.8
  • Qt 6.9.0 through Qt 6.11.1
  • Status unknown before 4.1.0

Fixed in Qt 6.8.9, 6.11.2, and 6.12.0 or later, which render iteratively. Patch sets are also published by Qt for the dev, 6.11, and 6.8 branches (see References).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When a Qt application loads an SVG file containing excessively deep element nesting, the Qt SVG module traverses the document tree recursively — while resolving paint servers, detecting cycles (detectCycles), rendering, and destroying the internal tree — without enforcing any recursion depth limit. Every nesting level consumes one C++ call frame, so a crafted document with thousands of nested elements exhausts the process call stack and the application segfaults. The fix replaces the recursive traversals with iterative loops and bounded depth handling.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
EDUCATIONAL ONLY — conceptual description, not a working exploit.

Attack chain:

  1. Attacker generates a tiny, valid SVG containing thousands of nested <g> elements (groups inside groups). Generation takes milliseconds; the file can be under 1 KB.
  2. The SVG reaches the victim through any channel: download, email attachment, icon asset, chat avatar.
  3. The Qt application parses and renders it. render(), paint-server resolution, and cleanup each recurse once per nesting level.
  4. Each level burns one stack frame. The finite call stack overflows → the process crashes (denial of service).

Vulnerable vs. fixed pattern (illustrative):

# VULNERABLE: unbounded recursion — nesting depth controls stack depth
def render(node):
    draw(node)
    for child in node.children:
        render(child)            # one stack frame per level

# FIXED: iterative traversal with a hard depth cap
def render(node, max_depth=100):
    stack = [(node, 0)]
    while stack:
        current, depth = stack.pop()
        if depth > max_depth:
            raise ValueError("SVG nesting too deep")
        draw(current)
        stack.extend((c, depth + 1) for c in current.children)

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Qt to 6.8.9, 6.11.2, or 6.12.0 or later (or apply the official qtsvg patch set for your branch).
  • Validate / sanitize SVG input: reject documents whose nesting depth exceeds a sane bound before parsing.
  • Enforce recursion depth limits anywhere your own code walks attacker-influenced document trees.
  • Restrict which SVG files users can load and prefer trusted sources for icons/assets.

docs.title: CVE-2026-88900 — Apache Camel JGroups: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 Product Apache Camel camel-jgroups component (4.0.0 through 4.22.0) Type Deserialization of Untrusted Data (CWE-502) Vector A network-adjacent attacker joins the JGroups cluster and sends one crafted message — no login needed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Apache Camel 4.0.0 through 4.22.0 (the camel-jgroups component). Fixed in 4.18.5, 4.22.1 and 4.23.0. Lines 4.14–4.17 and 4.19–4.21 are end of life — move to a supported release.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The JGroups consumer deserializes every incoming cluster message with a bare ObjectInputStream — no ObjectInputFilter allow-list. The default JGroups channel is unauthenticated UDP multicast, so anyone on the network can join the cluster and deliver an ObjectMessage. One crafted message triggers a Java deserialization gadget chain before Camel can inspect anything, giving remote code execution.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker joins the unauthenticated JGroups multicast channel on your network.
  2. Attacker sends one ObjectMessage carrying a serialized gadget chain.
  3. The consumer calls ObjectInputStream.readObject() with no filter.
  4. The gadget chain fires during deserialization — code runs with the app's privileges.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: an unfiltered "deserializer" that executes anything it is handed, versus a strict allow-list filter that rejects unknown classes. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade to Camel 4.18.5, 4.22.1 or 4.23.0 — these set a default ObjectInputFilter allow-list on the JGroups consumer. As defense in depth, set a JVM-wide serial filter with -Djdk.serialFilter (or jdk.serialFilter in java.security). Isolate the JGroups multicast traffic on a trusted network segment — the channel has no authentication of its own. Audit cluster membership and hunt for unexpected nodes.

docs.title: CVE-2026-92262 — MariaDB #mysql50# Table-Name Bypass
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical 9.9 (CVSS 3.1) Product MariaDB Server 10.6.1–10.6.27, 10.11.x–10.11.18, 11.4.x–11.4.12, 11.8.x–11.8.8, 12.3.x–12.3.2, 13.0.x–13.0.1 Type Filesystem encoding bypass → file read/write, crash, RCE Attack vector Network · low privileges (CREATE TABLE)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
MariaDB encodes special table names so they map to harmless filenames on disk. But names starting with the legacy #mysql50# prefix skip that encoding entirely:

def encode_name(name):
    if name.startswith("#mysql50#"):
        return name          # legacy shortcut — no encoding!
    return safe_encode(name)

An attacker creates a table named #mysql50#../../<path> and the raw, unencoded name becomes a real filesystem path outside the data directory — readable and writable as the database user.

docs.text:
poc.py is an educational illustration of the bypass vs the fix. It touches no database and writes no files.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. Attacker (low DB privileges) runs CREATE TABLE \#mysql50#../../tmp/x` (...)`.
  2. The unencoded name escapes the data directory.
  3. Attacker reads/writes files as the mysql user: exfiltration, corruption, crashes — and potentially remote code execution.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to a fixed release (10.6.28, 10.11.19, 11.4.13, 11.8.9, 12.3.3, or 13.0.2).
  • Restrict CREATE TABLE privileges (least privilege).
  • Audit existing schemas for table names starting with #mysql50#.

  4. The attacker's code runs as the victim (keys, backdoors, ransomware).

docs.title: Core Terminology
docs.text: Term Description Network Set of interconnected devices sharing resources. LAN (local) or WAN (wide area). Node Any device on the network: computer, router, switch. Protocol Rule set governing data transmission. Examples: TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP. Bandwidth Max data throughput, measured in bits per second (bps). Latency Time for a packet to travel from source to destination. Lower = faster. Packet Basic data unit. Contains payload + headers (source/destination addresses). Firewall Device or software controlling inbound/outbound traffic via security rules.

docs.title: OSI Model (7 Layers)
docs.text: # Layer Function Examples 7 Application User-facing services HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS 6 Presentation Data format translation, encryption SSL/TLS 5 Session Connection management between apps RPC 4 Transport Reliable end-to-end delivery TCP, UDP 3 Network Routing between networks IP, ICMP 2 Data Link Direct node-to-node transfer MAC, Ethernet 1 Physical Hardware transmission (cables, signals) Ethernet cables, USB

docs.title: TCP/IP Model (4 Layers)
docs.text: # Layer OSI Equivalent Examples 4 Application App + Presentation + Session HTTP, FTP, DNS 3 Transport Transport TCP, UDP 2 Internet Network IP, ICMP 1 Network Access Data Link + Physical Ethernet, Wi-Fi

docs.title: Subnetting & CIDR
docs.text:
• IP Address: Unique device identifier. IPv4 (192.168.1.1) or IPv6 (2001:db8::1).
  • Subnet Mask: Separates network vs host portion of an IP. Common: 255.255.255.0.
  • CIDR: Compact notation — 192.168.1.0/24 means 24 bits for network, 8 for hosts.

docs.title: Subnetting benefits
docs.text:
• Security — isolate network segments, limit blast radius
  • Efficiency — avoid IP waste on large flat networks
  • Traffic reduction — local traffic stays within subnet

docs.title: Assessment Methodologies
docs.text: Structured approach to security assessments — from passive recon through vulnerability scanning.

docs.title: 1. Passive Information Gathering
docs.text:
Collect data about the target without direct interaction. Uses public sources only — no packets sent to the target.

Tool Purpose DNSRecon DNS record enumeration (A, MX, NS, TXT, zone transfer attempts) whois Domain ownership, registration dates, registrar, DNS servers DNSDumpster Visual DNS map — subdomains, IPs, MX, NS records Shodan Internet-connected device search; find exposed services Netcraft Web server history, technology stack, WHOIS reports Sublist3r Subdomain enumeration via search engines and APIs theHarvester Email, host, and subdomain discovery from public sources 
# Passive DNS recon
dnsrecon -d target.com
whois target.com
theHarvester -d target.com -b all

docs.title: 2. Service Discovery
docs.text:
Identify active hosts and open ports on the target network.

Tool Purpose nmap Port scanning, service detection, OS fingerprinting netcat Manual port probing, banner grabbing masscan High-speed port scanning across large ranges 
# Discover live hosts
nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

# Fast full port scan
nmap -p- --open --min-rate 5000 -n -Pn <target>

# Service + version detection
nmap -sCV -p<ports> <target>

docs.title: 3. Service Enumeration
docs.text:
Enumerate services in depth to extract versions, configurations, and potential entry points.

Tool Purpose nmap -sCV Script scan + version detection on open ports nikto Web server vulnerability scanner gobuster / ffuf Web directory and file brute force enum4linux SMB/Samba enumeration (users, shares, policies) 
# Web enumeration
nikto -h http://target.com
gobuster dir -u http://target.com -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

# SMB enumeration
enum4linux -a target.com

docs.title: 4. Vulnerability Scanning
docs.text:
Scan discovered services for known CVEs and misconfigurations.

Tool Purpose OpenVAS Open-source full vulnerability scanner Nessus Commercial vulnerability scanner (widely used) nmap NSE Script-based vuln checks (--script vuln) 
# Nmap vuln scripts
nmap --script vuln -p<ports> <target>

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text:
1. whois + DNSRecon + theHarvester   → passive recon
2. nmap -sn                           → host discovery
3. nmap -p- --min-rate 5000           → port discovery
4. nmap -sCV -p<ports>                → service fingerprinting
5. nikto / gobuster / enum4linux      → service enumeration
6. OpenVAS / Nessus / nmap --script vuln → vulnerability scan

docs.title: DNSRecon
docs.text:
Open-source DNS enumeration and security auditing tool. Performs detailed DNS queries to map domain infrastructure and detect misconfigurations.

GitHub: https://github.com/darkoperator/dnsrecon

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
sudo apt install dnsrecon
# or
pip3 install dnsrecon

docs.title: What it finds
docs.text: Record type Description A / AAAA IPv4 / IPv6 addresses MX Mail servers NS Name servers TXT SPF, DKIM, verification records SOA Start of Authority — zone info Zone transfer Full DNS zone dump (if server misconfigured) Subdomains Via brute-force wordlist Reverse DNS IP → hostname resolution

docs.title: Core commands
docs.text:
# Standard record enumeration
dnsrecon -d example.com

# Zone transfer attempt
dnsrecon -d example.com -t axfr

# Subdomain brute force
dnsrecon -d example.com -t brt

# Reverse DNS sweep on a range
dnsrecon -r 192.168.1.0/24 -t rvl

# Google enumeration
dnsrecon -d example.com -t goo

# Save results to JSON
dnsrecon -d example.com -j output.json

# Save results to CSV
dnsrecon -d example.com --csv output.csv

docs.title: Scan types (-t)
docs.text: Type Description std Standard record lookup (default) axfr Zone transfer attempt brt Brute-force subdomain enumeration goo Google scraping for subdomains rvl Reverse lookup on IP range snoop Cache snooping against nameserver tld TLD expansion

docs.title: Complementary tools
docs.text: Tool Use dig Manual DNS query with fine-grained control fierce Subdomain-focused DNS scanner nmap Port/service scan after DNS recon dnsdumpster.com Visual passive DNS map subfinder Fast passive subdomain enumeration

docs.title: HTTrack
docs.text:
Open-source website crawler and offline browser. Downloads complete websites — HTML, CSS, JS, images — for offline analysis.

GitHub: https://github.com/xroche/httrack Official site: https://www.httrack.com

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: sudo apt install httrack

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Clone a full website
httrack "https://example.com" -O "/path/to/output/"

# Limit crawl depth
httrack "https://example.com" -O "/path/to/output/" -r2

# Exclude specific file types
httrack "https://example.com" -O "/path/to/output/" -*.png -*.jpg

# Mirror with no external links
httrack "https://example.com" -O "/path/to/output/" -%e0

Passive subdomain enumeration tool. Queries search engines and public APIs to build a subdomain list without directly probing the target.

sublist3r -d example.com

docs.text: Protocol and command-line tool for querying public registration databases. Returns ownership, registration dates, DNS servers, and contact info for domains and IP ranges.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Pre-installed on most Linux/macOS systems. On Debian/Ubuntu: 

sudo apt install whois

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Domain lookup
whois example.com

# IP address lookup
whois 8.8.8.8

# Specific WHOIS server
whois -h whois.arin.net 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Key fields in output
docs.text: Field Description Domain Name Queried domain Registry Domain ID Unique domain identifier in registry Registrar Organization managing the registration Creation Date When the domain was first registered Expiration Date When registration expires Updated Date Last modification date Name Servers DNS servers authoritative for the domain Status Domain state (active, clientHold, pendingDelete, etc.) Registrant Owner name/org (often redacted for privacy) Admin / Tech Email Contact emails (often redacted)

docs.title: IP WHOIS
docs.text:
whois 8.8.8.8
# Returns: ASN, netblock owner (Google), country, abuse contact

Regional registries (ARIN, RIPE, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC) hold IP block data.

docs.title: What to look for during recon
docs.text:
whois target.com | grep -iE "registrar|name server|creation|expir|registrant|email|phone"
  • Registrar → hosting/registrar relationship
  • Name servers → often reveals CDN, hosting provider, or managed DNS
  • Creation date → very new domain = higher risk of phishing
  • Expiry soon → potential for domain hijacking
  • Contact emails → useful for social engineering scope or OSINT

dig target.com ANY
nslookup -type=mx target.com

docs.title: WafW00f
docs.text:
WAF (Web Application Firewall) detection tool. Sends crafted requests to a target and analyzes responses to identify the WAF protecting it.

GitHub: https://github.com/EnableSecurity/wafw00f

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install wafw00f
# or
sudo apt install wafw00f

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Detect WAF on a target
wafw00f https://example.com

# Test all known WAFs (slower but more thorough)
wafw00f -a https://example.com

# Verbose output
wafw00f -v https://example.com

# Output in JSON
wafw00f -o output.json https://example.com

# Test multiple targets from file
wafw00f -i targets.txt

docs.title: What it detects
docs.text:
WafW00f fingerprints 100+ WAFs including:

WAF Vendor Cloudflare Cloudflare AWS WAF Amazon ModSecurity Open Source Akamai Kona Akamai Imperva Incapsula Imperva F5 BIG-IP ASM F5 Barracuda WAF Barracuda Sucuri Sucuri 
# Example output
[*] Checking https://example.com
[+] The site https://example.com is behind Cloudflare (Cloudflare Inc.) WAF.
[~] Number of requests: 7

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Sends normal baseline request
  2. Sends crafted malicious payloads (SQLi, XSS probes)
  3. Compares response headers, body, and status codes
  4. Matches patterns against WAF signature database

docs.title: Use in pentesting
docs.text:
• Before active testing — know if WAF is present; adjust payloads accordingly
  • WAF bypass planning — identify WAF type → research known bypass techniques
  • Scope documentation — document security controls in pentest report

docs.title: DNSDumpster
docs.text:
Web-based passive DNS reconnaissance tool. Maps DNS infrastructure of a target domain using public data — no direct contact with target servers.

URL: https://dnsdumpster.com

docs.title: What it finds
docs.text: Record type Info A IPv4 addresses for the domain and subdomains MX Mail servers NS Name servers TXT SPF, DKIM, and other TXT records Subdomains Associated subdomains discovered from public sources IP geolocation Country/region for each IP

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
1. Go to https://dnsdumpster.com
  2. Enter domain (e.g. example.com)
  3. Results show DNS records, subdomain map, and IP distribution
  4. Export as PDF for offline analysis

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• Passive only — no requests sent to target; reduces detection risk
  • Free — no account required
  • Visual output — infrastructure map showing how DNS components relate
  • Fast — results in seconds

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Subdomain discovery before active testing
  • Identify mail/name servers for phishing simulation scope
  • Map attack surface during initial recon phase

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Coverage depends on public data sources — may miss recent subdomains
  • No brute-force capability (use subfinder, amass, or dnsrecon -t brt for that)
  • Rate-limited on free tier
